title: Narrow immoral-law validity and separately review ordinary-injustice evidence
author: Worldview Sorter jurisprudence review
currentBehavior: Release 1.20 uses PLI071@1 and PLI073@1. PLI073:not_law opposes the ordinary-validity rule, so a threshold response can produce a spurious mixed state. The incomplete 1.21 attempt removed that opposition without replacing the second opposing unit, making the rule not_measured for every profile. Its proposed social-sources primacy clause also exceeded the evidence.
proposedBehavior: Use exactly 'An immoral law can remain legally valid.' PLI071@1 remains unchanged. Separately add PLI128@1: an unfair city fee satisfies all institutional validity criteria including incorporated moral conditions, while its injustice is stipulated below an intolerable extreme threshold. PLI071 agreement and PLI128:valid_but_unjust support; PLI071 disagreement and PLI128:not_law oppose. The latter explicitly denies that an immoral rule can remain valid even below that threshold. PLI128:defective_law/depends are nondirectional. Remove PLI073 entirely from this rule. Preserve two distinct supporting and opposing units and every existing gate.
rationale: A moral-fallibility proposition does not establish social-sources primacy or legal positivism. A separately authored ordinary-injustice case restores bidirectional coverage without treating extreme-threshold invalidity as opposition. Distinct authored units are software evidence units, not a claim of empirical independence or psychometric validation.

philosophicalBasis.proposition: An immoral law can remain legally valid.
neighboringViews: Inclusive positivism allows incorporated moral validity criteria, explicitly satisfied in PLI128.
Exclusive positivism endorses a stronger sources thesis not established by this proposition.
Threshold natural-law views can accept ordinary immoral laws while rejecting extreme injustice.
Finnis-style defective law can retain technical validity.
Moral duty to obey or enforce is distinct from legal validity.
nonEntailments: Legal validity depends primarily or exclusively on social sources.
A positivist identity, inclusive or exclusive.
A denial that extreme injustice can invalidate an enactment.
A moral obligation to obey, enforce, or approve every valid law.
All immoral laws are valid, or incorporated moral criteria are irrelevant.
philosophicalBasis.existingGap: The incomplete mapping had only one opposing unit. PLI128 supplies a separately reviewed, original ordinary-injustice unit in both directions; PLI073 no longer supplies either direction. False positives from institutional moral invalidity, extreme-threshold rejection and undefined defective-law language are excluded rather than assigned philosophical identities.
philosophicalBasis.scholarlyDisagreement: SEP Legal Positivism section 4.1 explicitly says moral fallibility is not exclusive to positivism and is accepted by several natural-law and nonpositivist accounts. SEP Natural Law Theories section 4 distinguishes technical validity from lack of moral directiveness and focal defectiveness. These limited claims support the narrowed proposition, not a stronger theory of legal sources.

sourceClaims.claim: Legal Positivism, section 4.1, states that law can be morally deficient and that this moral-fallibility thesis is not the exclusive property of positivism; accepting immoral law therefore does not establish social-sources primacy or a positivist identity.

Natural Law Theories, section 4, permits saying that a rule is legally valid yet too unjust to obey or apply, while distinguishing its defective or non-central sense. Technical validity, moral directiveness and focal defectiveness must not be collapsed.
Bibliographic lead for the separation debate; this article was not read in this review. The modest moral-fallibility claim relies on the reviewed SEP synthesis, not an asserted direct reading.
Bibliographic lead for the extreme-injustice threshold debate; the primary text was not read in this review. No exhaustive reconstruction of the formula is claimed by the ordinary-injustice item.

alternatives: Keep PLI073:not_law as opposition: rejected because extreme-threshold rejection does not deny ordinary immoral-law validity.
Remove only that opposition: rejected because it leaves one opposing unit and disables measurement.
Weaken minimumEvidenceUnits or directional availability gates: rejected.
Claim social-sources primacy from PLI071: rejected as a stronger proposition than the item supports.
respondentImpact: Full adds PLI128@1 alongside MCP-2026-096's PLI072@2, reaching 253 items and 99 assessable direct rules; bank 578. Quick/Standard references, affinity criteria, identity gates and scoring thresholds are unchanged. Coherent threshold fixtures can support both narrow propositions without being assigned a tradition.
historicalCompatibility: Release 1.20 keeps its original model, route, bank and engine. Its PLI071@1/PLI073@1 answers replay under the historical mapping, including the historical mixed state. Successor interpretations are separately versioned and do not transfer PLI073@1 answers to revised wording or to PLI128.

Four primary/book leads remain unread; no human, independent psychometric or empirical validation is claimed.
